title: A Salmon Farm in Maine Paused Its $300 Million Project — and Blames Tariffs
summary: Millinocket, Maine, used to be a paper mill town. When the mill closed in 2008, the town of about 4,100 people struggled. Then came big news: a $300 million salmon farming project, backed partly by Norwegian investors, planned to reuse the old mill's giant lagoons. It was called Great Northern Salmon. "It was a marriage made in heaven," said Gail Fanjoy, president of the local chamber of commerce. The project was about 80 percent done when the company announced last month it was pausing indefinitely. The reason? Uncertainty caused by President Trump's tariffs. Much of the salmon equipment was going to be imported from Canada. "The Norwegian investors just said, 'We're done, we just can't deal with this,'" Fanjoy said. Maine does $6 billion in two-way trade with Canada every year — a lot for a state smaller than Manitoba. The tariffs are a big issue in Maine's Senate race. Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has held her seat for 30 years, is running for re-election. Asked if tariffs could hurt her chances, she said she's more worried about the people of Maine. "Canada's our friend, our neighbour, our biggest trading partner," she said. She urged both sides to negotiate.
why_it_matters: When leaders far away make decisions about taxes on trade, small towns can lose the new jobs they were counting on, so trade news matters even to families far from Washington.

background_read: Millinocket is a small town in the U.S. state of Maine, right next to Canada (the country just north of the United States).
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) has put tariffs — extra taxes on goods from other countries — on many products, including some from Canada.

Norway (a country in northern Europe) is one of the world's biggest salmon farmers, raising fish in nets in the sea, and Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has held her Maine Senate seat for 30 years, is running for re-election as trade with Canada becomes a big issue.
Article_Structure: WHO: The town of Millinocket, Maine, the company Great Northern Salmon, Norwegian investors, and Sen. Susan Collins.
WHAT: A $300 million salmon farm that was about 80 percent done was paused indefinitely because of tariff uncertainty, since much equipment came from Canada.
WHERE: Millinocket, Maine, in the United States, with equipment coming from Canada.
WHY: The Norwegian investors said they couldn't deal with the tariff situation, and the tariffs are now a major issue in Maine's Senate race.

perspectives.description: Gail Fanjoy of the local chamber of commerce called the salmon project 'a marriage made in heaven' — a way to bring jobs back to a town that lost its paper mill.
The Norwegian investors walked away from a project that was nearly finished, saying they simply couldn't deal with the tariff uncertainty.
Sen. Susan Collins says she is more worried about the people of Maine than her own election, and she wants both sides to negotiate so trade can go back to normal.
